:::{#def-notational-shorthand}
#### Notational shorthand

A **notational shorthand** is a way of writing an expression
that leaves part of the expression out,
such as the set a sum runs over or the limits of an integral,
and relies on the reader to supply the missing part from context.
The expression with every part written out is its **full form**.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {.callout-note}
#### These notes write the full form

In these notes,
we avoid notational shorthands in permanent writing
and write the full form of each expression,
even where a shorthand would be shorter.
A reader who supplies the missing part of a shorthand
from a different context than the writer intended
reads a different expression than the one the writer meant.
Handwritten board work is often less complete,
but it should still write out ranges and limits where it can.

We make one exception:
writing two factors side by side means multiplying them,
as in $2x$ for $2 \cd x$ and $ab$ for $a \cd b$.
We still write the multiplication sign
when the side-by-side form could be misread:

- $2 \cd 3$, not $23$, which reads as twenty-three;
- $a \cd (b + c)$ when $a$ could be a function,
  since $a(b + c)$ could mean $a$ evaluated at $b + c$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-range-of-variable}
#### Range of a variable

The **range** of a variable $x$, written $\rangef{x}$,
is the set of values that $x$ can take.

:::

For example,
if $x$ is the number of heads in two tosses of a coin,
then $\rangef{x} = \cb{0, 1, 2}$.
A [random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-random-variable) $X$
(defined in the Morrison Lab's probability notes)
is a [function](sets-functions.qmd#def-function),
and the set of values $X$ can take, $\rangef{X}$,
is the [image](sets-functions.qmd#def-image) of $X$.
These notes use "range" only for variables:
for a function, "range" can mean either the image or the codomain
([Image and range](sets-functions.qmd#rem-image-range)).
In statistics, "the range" of a dataset can also mean
its largest value minus its smallest value;
$\rangef{x}$ is a set, not that difference.

{{< slidebreak >}}

@tbl-notational-shorthands lists shorthands you may meet in other sources,
the full form each one abbreviates,
and the part each one leaves out.
In the table,
$x_1, \ldots, x_n$ and $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are $n$ numbers,
$b_{ij}$ is the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ of an $m \times n$ array,
$k$ is an integer with $1 \le k \le n$,
$f$ is a [function](sets-functions.qmd#def-function)
from $\reals$ to $\reals$,
and, in the first row, $\rangef{x}$ is a finite set.

| Shorthand | Full form | Part left out |
|:----------|:----------|:--------------|
| $\sum_{x} f(x)$ | $\sum_{x \in \rangef{x}} f(x)$ | the set the sum runs over ([sum over a finite set](algebra.qmd#def-sum-over-set)) |
| $\sum_{i} x_i$ | $\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ | the lower and upper limits of the index ([summation notation](algebra.qmd#def-summation)) |
| $\sum x_i$ | $\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ | the index and its lower and upper limits |
| $\prod_{i} x_i$ | $\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ | the lower and upper limits of the index |
| $\prod x_i$ | $\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ | the index and its lower and upper limits |
| $\sum_{i, j} b_{ij}$ | $\sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} b_{ij}$ | the limits of both indices |
| $\sum_{i \neq k} a_i$ | $\sum_{i \in \cb{1, \ldots, n} \setminus \cb{k}} a_i$ | the set $\cb{1, \ldots, n}$ of indices that $k$ is removed from |
| $\int f(x)\,dx$, used for a number | $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$ | the limits of integration |
| $\int f$ | $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$ | the limits, the variable of integration, and the differential $dx$ |
| $x_{1:n}$ | $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$ | the explicit list of entries |
| "the function $x^2$" | "the function $f : \reals \to \reals$ with $f(x) = x^2$" | the function's name, domain, and codomain |

: Common notational shorthands and their full forms {#tbl-notational-shorthands}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-indefinite-integral-not-shorthand}
#### $\int f(x)\,dx$ has two readings

In calculus,
$\int f(x)\,dx$ with no limits is not a shorthand:
it is the [indefinite integral](calculus.qmd#def-indefinite-integral) of $f$,
a family of functions rather than a number.
Some sources, especially in probability,
also write $\int f(x)\,dx$ for the number $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$.
Writing the limits out tells the reader which of the two is meant.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-expand-index-shorthand}
#### Writing out an index shorthand

Let $n = 3$ and $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (2, 5, 1)$.
A source that writes $\sum_{i} x_i$ means $\sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i$:

$$
\ba
\sum_{i=1}^{3} x_i
&= x_1 + x_2 + x_3
&& \text{(definition of summation notation)} \\
&= 2 + 5 + 1
&& \text{(substitute the values)} \\
&= 8
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

:::
